The Discussion on Matter as Karma.
Is bodily karma originated by a wholesome consciousness wholesome matter? Yes.
“Does it have an object? Is there for it turning toward, mental advertence, attention, volition, aspiration, and resolve?
“One should not say so.
“… [As before] …” “Is it then without an object? Is there for it no turning toward, mental advertence, attention, volition, aspiration, or resolve?”
“Yes,” he says.
“If it is without an object, then there is for it no turning toward [the object], nor... nor aspiration. Therefore, indeed, you should not say:
“Bodily action originated by a wholesome mind is wholesome matter.”
If contact arisen from a wholesome mind is wholesome and has an object, and it possesses turning toward [the object]... up to ...
aspiration, then is bodily action as form, which is arisen from a wholesome mind, also wholesome and has an object, and does it possess turning toward [the object]... up to ... aspiration? Yes.
It should not be said thus ... pe ...
feeling arisen from a wholesome mind ... pe ... perception ... pe ... [should not be said thus].
volition … faith … energy …
When there is mindfulness … concentration … [and so on] … wisdom that is wholesome and has an object, is there turning toward it … [and so on] … aspiration for it?
“Yes,” you say.
“Is bodily action originated by a wholesome mind—being material form that is wholesome and with an object—possessing turning toward … [and so on] … up to … having aspiration?
You should not speak thus … [and so on].

Is bodily action (kāyakamma) that has arisen from a wholesome mind (kusala-citta) wholesome matter (rūpa), without an object (anārammaṇa), and for which there is no turning back (āvaṭṭanā) … [and so on] … nor aspiration (paṇidhi)?
Yes. Is contact (phassa) that has arisen from a wholesome mind wholesome, without an object, and for which there is no turning back … [and so on] … nor aspiration? Yes.

It should not be said thus … [as before] … “Is bodily action originated by a wholesome consciousness wholesome matter that is without an object, and for which there is no turning toward, … [and so on] … no aspiration?
Yes.
Feeling arisen from a wholesome mind … perception … volition … [and so on].
faith … energy … mindfulness …

One should not say so … pe ….
Is bodily action originated by a wholesome mind wholesome matter?
Yes. Is all matter whatsoever originated by a wholesome mind wholesome? No.

Yes.

Indeed, you should not say:”
“Bodily action originated by a wholesome mind is wholesome matter.
Is contact originated by a wholesome mind wholesome and possessed of an object; does it have turning toward [the object], and so forth, up to aspiration?
Yes.

Is verbal action (vacīkamma) that has arisen from a wholesome mind (kusala-citta)—being material form (rūpa), wholesome, and with an object—possess turning toward [the object] …pe… and aspiration (paṇidhi)?
It should not be said so …pe… [Is] feeling (vedanā) that has arisen from a wholesome mind …pe… [similarly]? It should not be said so.
perception … volition … faith …

Is verbal action originating from a wholesome mind—being material form—wholesome and with an object, and does it have turning toward [the object], and so forth, up to aspiration? [No.]

It should not be said so … [as before] … Is verbal action originated by a wholesome consciousness wholesome matter that is without an object, and for which there is no turning toward, … [and so on] … no aspiration?

Yes. Does it have an object; does it possess turning toward it, mental advertence, attention, mental application, volition, aspiration, and resolve? Yes.

[as before] ...Is it not the case that [this state] is without an object, and that for it there is no turning toward, no mental advertence, no attention, no mental orientation, no volition, no aspiration, and no resolve?
Yes, it is.
If it is without an object, then for it there is no turning toward, no mental advertence, no attention, no mental application, no volition, no aspiration, and no resolve.
In that case, indeed, you must not say:
"Bodily action originated by an unwholesome mind is unwholesome matter."
Is contact originated by an unwholesome mind unwholesome, with an object, and does it have turning toward, [and so on] … up to … aspiration?
Yes. Is bodily action, which is material form originated by an unwholesome mind, unwholesome, with an object, and does it have turning toward, [and so on] … up to … aspiration? Yes.

volition … lust … hatred …

One should not say so...

Is bodily action originated by an unwholesome mind—being unwholesome material form without an object—not possessed of turning toward [the object], and so forth, up to aspiration? One should not say so either... [and so on].
“Yes,” you say.

You should not speak thus … [and so forth] … No, indeed.
Is bodily action arisen from an unwholesome mind—being material form (rūpa)—unwholesome and without an object, and does it lack turning toward [the object], and so on, up to aspiration?
Yes. Is feeling arisen from an unwholesome mind likewise [unwholesome and without an object]...? Yes.

[and no] aspiration? Yes.

If bodily action and verbal action are both wholesome and unwholesome, then indeed, sir, you must say:
"Material form is both wholesome and unwholesome.
Is material form both wholesome and unwholesome?

“Then is the eye-base both wholesome and unwholesome?
You should not say so … [and so on] …

Yes. Is the ear-base … [and so on] …?

“But has it not been said by the Blessed One:
‘Bhikkhus, I say that volition is action’?”
“Having willed, one performs action by way of body, speech, and mind.
Is this indeed a sutta?
Yes, it is.
Therefore, it should not be said that "form is karma.
Is form karma?
“Yes, [it is so].
“But was it not said by the Blessed One:
‘Ānanda, when there is a body, bodily volition arises as a cause for the arising of pleasure and pain within oneself’?”
“Or, Ānanda, when there is speech, internal pleasure and pain arise with volition regarding speech as their cause;
or, Ānanda, when there is mind, internal pleasure and pain arise with volition regarding the mind as their cause.
Is this indeed a sutta?
“Yes,” [you say].
In that case, it should not be said that “form is karma.”
Is form karma?
Yes. Has it not been said by the Blessed One:
“Monks, threefold is bodily volition: unwholesome bodily action with suffering as its outcome and suffering as its result.
Monks, fourfold is verbal volition: unwholesome verbal action with suffering as its outcome and suffering as its result.
Monks, threefold is mental volition: unwholesome mental action with suffering as its outcome and suffering as its result.”
“Bhikkhus, threefold is bodily volition: wholesome bodily action with a pleasant outcome and a pleasant result.
Bhikkhus, fourfold is verbal volition: wholesome verbal action with a pleasant outcome and a pleasant result.
Bhikkhus, threefold is mental volition: wholesome mental action with a pleasant outcome and a pleasant result.”
Is it indeed a sutta? Yes.
Therefore, it should not be said—
“Form is action.
Is form action? Yes.
Has it not been said by the Blessed One:
"If, Ānanda, this foolish man Samiddhi, being asked thus by the wanderer of Pāṭaliputta, were to answer thus:
'Friend Pāṭaliputta, having performed an intentional deed through body, speech, or mind to be experienced as pleasant, he experiences pleasure;'"
“Friend Pāṭaliputta, having performed an intentional deed by way of body, speech, or mind that is to be experienced as painful, he experiences pain;
friend Pāṭaliputta, having performed an intentional deed by way of body, speech, or mind that is to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, he experiences neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
If, Ānanda, the foolish man Samiddhi were to answer in this way, [he would be speaking correctly].
“If one were to answer correctly for the wanderer of Pāṭaliputta, one would answer thus.
Is this indeed a sutta? Yes.
Therefore, it should not be said that "form is karma.
The discussion on whether form is karma is concluded.
